title: NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet Multiplane Network Architecture at Hot Chips 2026
gist: Nvidia detailed how its Spectrum-X multiplane Ethernet topology extends AI factory scale-out from roughly 8k to 512k Rubin GPUs (a 64x jump over multi-rail) while cutting scale-out switch count 1.7x and holding 90% bandwidth under partial failure (versus 0% for traditional multi-tier topologies), reinforcing Nvidia's thesis that AI networking must be split into five purpose-built fabrics (scale-up, scale-out, scale-across, scale-in, and context scale) rather than served by one general-purpose network — directly contradicting Broadcom's unified-Ethernet pitch shown earlier the same day.

insights.claim: Nvidia's core architectural thesis is that AI factories require five distinct purpose-built networks — scale-up, scale-out, scale-across, scale-in, and 'AI context scale' — because a single general-purpose fabric cannot serve all of these needs well.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: This is the load-bearing claim of Nvidia's entire networking strategy and directly underpins sales of differentiated silicon (NVLink, Spectrum-X, BlueField, Astra) per network tier rather than a single commodity fabric — a structural argument for why Nvidia can maintain higher blended networking ASPs than a unified-Ethernet competitor.
insights.quote: A single general-purpose fabric cannot serve all of these well, and that is the load-bearing claim behind the rest of the talk.
insights.locator: AI Factories Need Five Purpose-Built Networks

insights.claim: Nvidia's five-network framing (with 'scale-in' introduced as a new category) directly contradicts Broadcom's Thor Ultra pitch earlier the same Hot Chips day, which argued a shared/unified NIC requirement set could serve scale-up, scale-out, and scale-across together.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A direct, same-day strategic disagreement between the two largest AI networking vendors is a rare, clean signal of the real industry debate over network architecture — investors should watch actual hyperscaler network deployments (not vendor claims) to see which philosophy wins design wins.
insights.quote: it was a bit awkward watching Broadcom's Thor Ultra presentation today knowing that scale-in was going to become a thing in the subsequent presentation.
insights.locator: AI Factories Need Five Purpose-Built Networks

insights.claim: The author's closing assessment is skeptical/neutral: Nvidia is arguing Ethernet can handle AI factory scale-out only when hardware is purpose-built for AI, and 'whether those figures hold in live deployments is the real test' — i.e., the claims are unproven outside NVIDIA's own benchmarks.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A direct caution against taking Nvidia's multiplane performance multipliers at face value; investors should wait for independent/hyperscaler-reported deployment data before treating the 64x scale claim as validated.
insights.quote: Whether those figures hold in live deployments is the real test, and the rest of Hot Chips should show how the Vera Rubin software-and-optics story comes together.

themes.theme: Multiplane topology: the headline scaling claim

insights.claim: Nvidia's new multiplane Ethernet topology connects each NIC to multiple switches (8x 200Gbps links to 8 different switches instead of 1.6Tbps to a single switch as in multi-rail), and this design extends AI factory scale by 64x over multi-rail, reaching 512k Rubin GPUs versus roughly 8k GPUs for multi-rail, while maintaining 1.6T scale-out bandwidth per GPU.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A 64x scale-out ceiling increase (8k to 512k GPUs) is a massive claimed expansion in addressable cluster size for a single fabric — if realized, this materially raises the scale of frontier training runs achievable on Ethernet-based Nvidia infrastructure, a key input for forecasting the largest feasible AI training clusters over the next few years.
insights.quote: Multiplane extends AI factory scale by 64x over multi-rail. NVIDIA lands at 512k Rubin GPUs, still at 1.6T scale-out bandwidth per GPU.
insights.locator: Spectrum-X Ethernet Multiplane Extends AI-Factory Scale by 64X

insights.claim: The multiplane topology also reduces physical footprint, with Nvidia claiming 1.7x fewer scale-out switches than a traditional multi-tier single-rail topology, cutting power, rack space, and cost.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Fewer switches per GPU at equivalent bandwidth directly reduces networking capex and power overhead for hyperscalers building Rubin-generation clusters — a concrete efficiency lever for AI datacenter TCO modeling.
insights.quote: Multiplane also trims the physical footprint. NVIDIA claims 1.7x fewer scale-out switches than a traditional multi-tier single-rail topology.
insights.locator: Spectrum-X Ethernet Multiplane Saves 1.7x Scale-Out Switches

insights.claim: Under partial bandwidth loss (fault conditions), Nvidia's multiplane topology holds 90% of bandwidth with a 2.68ms detection time and about 100ms recovery time, versus a traditional multi-tier topology that drops to 0% bandwidth with 1080ms detection/recovery — a roughly 400x faster fault detection and 11x faster recovery, yielding a 1.6x goodput advantage over off-the-shelf Ethernet multiplane.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Fault resilience at this scale (90% bandwidth retained vs. total loss) is arguably more commercially important than peak throughput for hyperscalers running expensive, long-duration training jobs — network outages that used to stall entire jobs become minor, brief degradations, materially improving effective cluster utilization and reducing wasted GPU-hours.
insights.quote: Spectrum-X detects faults in 2.68ms, roughly 400x faster, and recovers in 100ms, about 11x faster, holding 90% bandwidth, whereas the OTS topology suffers full bandwidth loss with 1080ms detection and recovery.

themes.theme: Spectrum-X performance claims vs. off-the-shelf Ethernet

insights.claim: Nvidia claims Spectrum-X delivers 1.6x higher RDMA bandwidth, 2.2x better multi-tenancy, and 1.3x lower bandwidth jitter versus generic Ethernet around its 102.4T switch systems and 1.6T SuperNICs, framing jitter reduction as a full end-to-end system problem rather than a single-device fix.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Jitter and multi-tenancy isolation (not just raw bandwidth) are positioned as Nvidia's key differentiators — relevant for cloud providers running multiple AI customers on shared infrastructure, where noisy-neighbor effects can directly hurt SLA-bound training/inference performance.
insights.quote: NVIDIA claims 1.6x higher RDMA bandwidth, 2.2x better multi-tenancy, and 1.3x lower bandwidth jitter around 102.4T switch systems and 1.6T SuperNICs.

insights.claim: In a DeepSeek V3 multi-job training run on a noisy shared/multi-tenant environment, Nvidia measured 1.9x higher training performance versus off-the-shelf Ethernet, with the performance gap widening progressively across 80+ training steps, attributed to low-jitter communication and tenant noise isolation.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A widening performance gap over many steps in a real multi-tenant scenario (using a well-known open model, DeepSeek V3) suggests jitter/noise-isolation benefits compound over long training runs, making Spectrum-X's advantage more pronounced for longer/larger training jobs — directly relevant to any cloud provider hosting multiple concurrent AI training tenants.
insights.quote: step times for off-the-shelf Ethernet climb well above the Spectrum-X curves, with the gap widening across the 80-plus steps shown.
insights.locator: 1.9x Higher Training Performance in Multi-Tenant AI Factory

insights.claim: On Nemotron Ultra pre-training NCCL operations, Nvidia measured up to 14x higher performance for gradient all-reduce, 3.5x for token dispatch, and 2x for both gradient reduce-scatter and parallel matrix multiply, all relative to off-the-shelf Ethernet — described as evidence of 'extreme co-design.'
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A 14x gain on gradient all-reduce specifically is an extraordinarily large multiplier for a single collective operation — if real, this operation is often a critical-path bottleneck in large distributed training, so this claim (if it holds up) would represent one of the largest concrete network-driven training-speed advantages cited across this entire Hot Chips cycle.
insights.quote: gradient all-reduce leads at 14x, token dispatch sits at 3.5x, and both gradient reduce-scatter and parallel matrix multiply land at 2x, all relative to off-the-shelf Ethernet.

themes.theme: Optics: a rising and increasingly proprietary cost/power center

insights.claim: Nvidia states that optics account for about 10% of the compute power in an AI factory — well above what a conventional cloud data center typically carries — underscoring how much more optics-dependent scale-out AI networking is versus traditional cloud infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A 10% optics power share is a significant, likely under-appreciated cost/power line item in AI datacenter budgets; investors modeling AI datacenter power and capex should account for this rising optics burden, which benefits optics/photonics suppliers as scale-out networks grow.
insights.quote: NVIDIA puts the optical share in an AI factory at 10% of the compute power, well above what a conventional cloud data center typically carries.

insights.claim: Nvidia has a co-packaged optics chip with micro ring modulators already in production, plus a 3D-stacked silicon photonics engine on TSMC's Coupe process, claiming 4x fewer lasers, lower power, and 10x lower mean time between interruptions versus prior optics approaches.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Co-packaged optics moving to production (not just roadmap) on a dedicated TSMC process (Coupe) signals Nvidia is vertically integrating photonics manufacturing, a moat-building move that raises entry barriers for competitors and ties more of the AI networking supply chain to TSMC capacity.
insights.quote: NVIDIA has a co-packaged optics chip with micro ring modulators in production and a 3D-stacked silicon photonics engine on the TSMC Coupe process, and it claims 4x fewer lasers, lower power, and 10x lower mean time between interruptions.

insights.claim: Spectrum-XGS extends networking across multiple AI factories using 800Gb/s per port on 102.4Tb/s switches and ConnectX-9 SuperNICs, claiming up to 1.9x lower multi-site latency and doubled scale-across performance for distributed AI operations.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Cross-datacenter ('scale-across') networking is emerging as its own product category — relevant for tracking how hyperscalers may distribute massive training runs across multiple physical sites when a single datacenter's power/space constraints become binding.
insights.quote: NVIDIA claims up to 1.9x lower multi-site latency and doubled scale-across performance for distributed AI operations.

insights.claim: NVLink Fusion brings third-party XPUs onto the Nvidia AI platform, showing 3.6 TB/s all-to-all bandwidth per XPU connecting 72 XPUs in a single domain within a cableless MGX rack rated for 45C inlet and 100% liquid cooling, with 3x lower latency.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: NVLink Fusion opening to third-party XPUs (rather than only Nvidia GPUs) is a notable strategic hedge — it suggests Nvidia is positioning its interconnect IP as a platform for custom silicon vendors too, potentially capturing networking revenue even from hyperscalers building their own AI chips instead of losing them entirely to alternative fabrics.
insights.quote: NVLink Fusion brings third-party XPUs onto the NVIDIA AI platform.
insights.locator: NVLink Fusion Connects XPUs to the NVIDIA AI Platform

insights.claim: Nvidia's DSX Air software claims to compress AI factory deployment timelines dramatically: infrastructure bring-up from six months to one week, infrastructure software from three months to one week, and deployment from two weeks to one day.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: If accurate, this kind of deployment-time compression (24x on bring-up) would materially shorten the time from capex outlay to revenue-generating AI capacity coming online — a meaningful factor in modeling how quickly hyperscaler capex translates into usable compute.
insights.quote: NVIDIA shows infrastructure bring-up falling from six months to one week, infrastructure software from three months to one week, and deployment from two weeks to one day.
